::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Complete [Build a polymer corona](fit-f127-corona.qmd) first. Read
[Your first scattering model](first-model.qmd#reuse-the-graph-with-other-radii) if changing a parameter dictionary is
unfamiliar. You should know the purpose of least-squares residuals and
experimental uncertainties. This page runs from a fresh kernel in
`docs/tutorials` inside a repository checkout.
:::

We will fit one arm description: four freely joined cylinders. Keep the
topology fixed while the optimizer changes its physical parameters.

## Load the data

We use only the higher-q block of the merged F127 measurement, keeping its
intensities and uncertainties unchanged.

The data are from Dai and Olsen's
[F127 SANS example](https://github.com/olsenlabmit/Accelerated-SANS-Code/tree/7f8a4b2548702f6e47e989266365d3efd771df01/PluronicF-127)
([paper](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4SM01350F)); download the
[data](data/f127/F127_0_merged_1.txt) and [license](data/f127/LICENSE).
Use an environment with `pyseb`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `matplotlib`, `pandas`,
`plotly`, `usd-core`, `sympy`, and Jupyter installed.

{{< include _f127-setup.qmd >}}

## Evaluate the experimental ensemble

The direct pySEB call on the construction page evaluates one connected arm. For the experimental
micelle, we also include the core, interference between its attached arms,
and a distribution of core sizes. The folded helper evaluates that ensemble
quickly and checks its connected scattering against native pySEB graphs.

The optimizer will adjust eight shared parameters. `arm_Rg_A` describes the
whole arm; the helper converts it to the dimensions of four identical
cylinders. The attachment offset sets the anchor radius to
`core_radius + offset * arm_Rg`.

The folded cells below define the graph and checked ensemble evaluator.
They do not run earlier tutorial pages or earlier fits.

{{< include _f127-model.qmd >}}

{{< include _f127-view.qmd >}}

Here are the initial values and bounds for this fit. Scale and background
convert the model intensity to the measured intensity units; the contrast
multiplier adjusts the core's contribution relative to the arms.

```{python}
example_key = ("cylinder", 4)
initial_parameters = {
    "core_radius_A": 42.,
    "arm_Rg_A": 25.,
    "attachment_offset_over_Rg": 1.,
    "core_radius_CV": .15,
    "scale": .1,
    "background_cm^-1": .003,
    "core_to_corona_contrast_multiplier": 2.,
    "segment_aspect_ratio": 3.,       # cylinder length / diameter
}
lower_bounds = [20., 5., 0., .005, .0001, 0., .05, .25]
upper_bounds = [80., 80., 2., .45, 100., .2, 5., 4.]
```

The residual function is the connection to the experiment: evaluate the
model, subtract the measured intensity, and divide by its uncertainty.
SciPy changes the parameter values to reduce those residuals.

```{python}
def example_intensity(q_values, values):
    return kernel(q_values, values, *example_key)


def example_residual(values):
    return (example_intensity(q, values) - intensity) / sigma


example_optimizer = least_squares(
    example_residual,
    list(initial_parameters.values()),
    bounds=(lower_bounds, upper_bounds),
    x_scale="jac",
    max_nfev=2000,
)
example_fit = summarize_fit(*example_key, [example_optimizer])
```

This is one bounded optimization from one starting point. The [next page’s
comparison](compare-f127-coronas.qmd) repeats fits from several starting points. First, look at
the result of this single build-and-fit example.

```{python}
dense_q = np.geomspace(q.min(), q.max(), 450)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.5))
ax.errorbar(q, intensity, sigma, fmt="ko", ms=3, label="F127 data")
ax.plot(dense_q, example_intensity(dense_q, example_fit["p"]),
        label=f"Four-cylinder arms: reduced χ² = {example_fit['reduced_chi2']:.2f}")
ax.set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlabel=r"$q$ [Å$^{-1}$]",
       ylabel=r"$I(q)$ [cm$^{-1}$]", title="Fit the connected four-cylinder-arm model")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Inspect the fitted structure

Now put the fitted dimensions back into the graph. The shared
`structure_figure` helper returns geometry for the compact gallery layout;
`pyseb.visualize` provides the direct one-call display used on the
[construction page](fit-f127-corona.qmd). Each arm uses the same
fitted segment parameters. The integer arm count shown here is rounded from
the fitted mean core volume; the fitted curve averages over sizes and
conformations.

```{python}
example_radius = example_fit["p"][0]
example_arm_count = int(round(2*(4*np.pi*example_radius**3/3)/6283))
example_world, _ = build_graph(*example_key, arms=example_arm_count)
example_path = SCENE_DIR / "four-cylinder-example-fitted-micelle.usda"
example_options = pyseb.USDExportOptions(pyseb.LengthUnit.Angstrom)
example_options.seed = 127
example_options.surface_samples = 8
example_options.curve_samples = 48
example_options.layout_mode = pyseb.LayoutMode.Random
# A small orientation search keeps the extra unfolded view practical to export.
example_options.orientation_trials = 4
example_options.relaxation_sweeps = 0
example_options.color_overrides = {"core": (.95, .55, .15), "anchor": (.25, .65, .95)}
example_options.opacity_overrides = {"anchor": .25}
example_world.export_usd("micelle", str(example_path), fitted_parameters(example_fit), example_options)

compact_structure_view(
    example_world, fitted_parameters(example_fit), example_options,
    "The fitted four-cylinder-arm micelle").show(
    config={"displaylogo": False, "scrollZoom": True})
scene_link(example_path, "Download the fitted example as OpenUSD")
```

The central sphere is the core. The larger transparent sphere is the
zero-contrast anchor, whose surface supplies the arm attachment points.
This is a representative conformation of the fitted analytical model;
rotating or resampling it does not change the calculated curve.


## Continue

Before trying more models, inspect the residuals and fitted dimensions.
Then continue to [Compare corona models](compare-f127-coronas.qmd).
